overview: Saint Lucia’s island history reaches far beyond the independent state established in 1979. Archaeological sites preserve evidence of earlier craft and coastal life. French and British colonization brought plantation slavery, while struggles over freedom and self-government changed political institutions. Kwéyòl celebrations, scholarship and literature are continuing parts of this history.

periods.title: French settlement and imperial rivalry
periods.summary: French colonization took root around the mid-seventeenth century. Control subsequently changed between France and Britain.

periods.title: Revolutionary emancipation and war
periods.summary: French revolutionary abolition brought freedom into the struggle over the island. Formerly enslaved people fought to defend it against British forces.

periods.title: British conquest and re-enslavement
periods.summary: The British invasion of 1796 restored slavery. Resistance to conquest was also resistance to the loss of freedom.

periods.title: A brief return to French control
periods.summary: French administration returned briefly in 1802, before Britain retook control the following year.

periods.title: British occupation resumes
periods.summary: Britain restored its administration in 1803. A Crown Colony system followed in 1808, with legislation imposed through Orders in Council.

periods.title: Treaty confirms British rule
periods.summary: The 1814 settlement assigned Saint Lucia to Britain. Plantation slavery continued.

periods.title: Abolition followed by apprenticeship
periods.summary: Legal abolition in 1834 was followed by compulsory apprenticeship. Freedom from slavery did not immediately mean freedom from coerced estate labour.

periods.title: Apprenticeship ends
periods.summary: Apprenticeship ended in 1838, a distinct transition from the abolition of slavery four years earlier.

periods.title: A partly elected legislature
periods.summary: The 1925 elections returned three representatives to a council that also contained officials and appointed members.

periods.title: Adult suffrage and expanding self-government
periods.summary: Universal adult suffrage arrived in 1951. Ministerial government followed, and Saint Lucia gained a chief minister under the 1960 constitution.

periods.title: Associated statehood
periods.summary: Saint Lucia controlled its internal affairs, while Britain retained responsibility for defence and foreign affairs.

periods.title: Independent Saint Lucia
periods.summary: Independence began on 22 February 1979. The new constitution replaced the associated-state constitution of 1967.

items.text: At Morne Lezard, a 2002 survey recovered small chert flakes, blade tools and hammerstones in test pits above the Balenbouche River. These remains, alongside previously collected ground-stone axes, identify an area of stoneworking. Their concentration helps researchers study where tools were made, without identifying the makers from pottery labels alone.

At Saltibus Point, the team excavated shell tools, griddle fragments and bones of turtles and fish. A fragment of a spindle whorl and a shaped shell inlay added evidence of craft. The refuse deposit brings food preparation and manufacture into view together; some shell fragments initially described as scoops may instead be natural breakage.

sections.title: Work, slavery and the struggle for freedom

items.text: A government order of 1832 regulated the time enslaved plantation workers could spend cultivating allotted food plots. During the first twelve weeks of the harvest season it allowed every second Monday, followed by every Monday for the remaining forty weeks. The schedule expressly accommodated planters’ needs, exposing how control of working time reached into household subsistence.

The same order set Monday as market day. It treated workers who received statutory food rations differently from those cultivating allotted plots, and named particular holidays. These are rules prescribed by colonial authorities, not proof that every estate obeyed them or that enslaved people accepted the arrangements.

The people whom colonial accounts called brigands included Africans who had left plantations and lived in forests. In 1796, formerly enslaved defenders fought alongside French revolutionary forces against a British invasion that threatened renewed enslavement. Their struggle concerned personal freedom as well as imperial control; it was not yet the independence of the modern state.

Arthur Lewis, born in Castries, won a scholarship to Britain in 1932 and studied at the London School of Economics. His later university career included Manchester and Princeton. In 1979 he shared the economics prize for research into development, bringing questions about poorer countries into the centre of economic analysis.

Lewis examined economies where a large agricultural workforce coexisted with expanding capitalist industry. He also studied the terms on which countries exporting tropical products traded with industrial economies. These models asked how growth and its benefits were distributed across sectors and countries; they were analytical contributions, not a single technology invented on Saint Lucia.

Derek Walcott described an English-language education at Saint Mary’s College within a world shaped by French Creole, African rhythms and Catholic practice. His mother was a teacher and encouraged his writing. In his account, literary work grew through family, teachers, theatre and the multilingual life around him.

Discussing Omeros, Walcott said he wanted to celebrate the island and people he knew. He resisted describing the poem as a simple rewriting of the Odyssey: classical references mattered, but Caribbean lives had their own meanings. His 1992 literature prize recognized a career rooted in this creative engagement with history and place.

Researcher Winston Phulgence interviewed people involved in the Freedom Monument project. Debate over Ricky George’s design included whether a seated man conveyed resistance and why women’s participation was absent. The resulting discussion shows how public monuments select and interpret the past, rather than simply reproducing it.

La Rose and La Marguerite are flower societies whose preparations extend far beyond their August and October feast days. Groups organize singing and dancing gatherings in owned or rented halls, raising funds through refreshments and games. The chantwèl, or lead singer, sustains the performance and the gathering’s energy.

The societies maintain repertoires that include quadrilles, lancers and other dances. More spontaneous gatherings and the formal feast have different expectations. The Folk Research Centre does not claim a precise origin date for the festivals; their continuing importance rests on collective organization, musical skill and participation.

Jounen Kwéyòl brings language, food, dress, traditional practices and technology into public celebration. Host communities and activities across the country contribute to a month of cultural events around October’s international Creole observance. This work makes local knowledge something to teach and use, as well as something to remember.

The 1978 constitutional order records the Saint Lucian House of Assembly’s request for the independence arrangements. Its commencement date was 22 February 1979. Reading the document distinguishes the legal end of association with Britain from earlier steps toward internal self-government.

ending.text: British rule ended with independence in 1979. Saint Lucia continues as a nation, with living cultural institutions and traditions. The map’s separate Saint Lucia records are intervals of geographic coverage, not repeated endings of its people or society.
